hypothesis: The neuron responds strongly to high-contrast, monochromatic or grayscale images featuring a distinct, dark, elongated structure—typically a vertical or diagonal strip, silhouette, or segmented body—set against a uniform, grainy, or out-of-focus background of medium to light gray. The activating feature is consistently rendered in deep charcoal, black, or dark brown, creating a sharp dark-on-light polarity with the neutral, desaturated backdrop. The specific visual forms vary from biological shapes (spider abdomens, centipedes, bird silhouettes) to inanimate objects (matchsticks, vertical fabric seams, tool handles, or dark apertures), all sharing a linear or oblong geometry. The neuron remains invariant to the object's semantic identity, lighting direction, and surface texture, as long as the grayscale palette and strong tonal contrast are preserved. The dark feature typically spans 30–80% of the image's vertical axis and is centered or slightly offset within the frame.

The tail, extending to the bottom of the view, is a rusty reddish-brown and is deeply forked, though the very ends are cut off by the lower boundary. The texture of the image is coarse, with visible monochromatic noise in the gray sky, and the lighting is diffuse, emphasizing the silhouette and the color variation between the dark body, white wing patches, and rufous tail.
